title: Examples and Applications
key_idea: Inclusion-exclusion gives powerful closed forms when $f_{\geq}(T)$ has special structure: (1) if it depends only on $|T|$, finite differences give $a(m)$ cleanly; (2) if it **factors** over an ordered set, the I-E sum becomes a **determinant**. The descent-set example leads to determinantal formulas (Eqs. 2.15–2.17) and a $q$-analogue tracking the inversion statistic (Eqs. 2.18–2.21).
summary:
This section works through major examples:

**Derangements** $D(n)$: the symmetric I-E with $b(k) = (n-k)!$ gives $D(n) = n! \sum_{j=0}^n (-1)^j/j!$. There is also a recurrence $D(n) = (n-1)(D(n-1)+D(n-2))$ with bijective proof.

**Descent-set counting**: For $w \in S_n$, define $\text{Des}(w) \subseteq [n-1]$. The 'at-least' count $\alpha_n(S)$ is a multinomial coefficient; the 'exact' count $\beta_n(S)$ is recovered by I-E. The key step is that $f_{\leq}(S) = \alpha_n(S)$ factors into a ratio of factorials that, after the I-E alternating sum, equals a **determinant** (Eqs. 2.15–2.17).

**q-analogue**: Weighting by $q^{\text{inv}(w)}$ gives $q$-multinomials and a $q$-determinant (Eqs. 2.18–2.21).

**Proposition 2.2.6**: Abstract condition under which $f_{=}$ is a determinant.

notation.description: Number of $w \in S_n$ with $\text{Des}(w) \subseteq S$ ('at least' descent set contained in $S$)
Number of $w \in S_n$ with $\text{Des}(w) = S$ (descent set exactly $S$)
In symmetric I-E: number of objects with 'at least $k$' (or $k$ or more) of a property
Multinomial coefficient $n!/(c_1! c_2! \cdots)$ where $\sum c_i = n$
Number of inversions of $w$: $|\{(i,j): i<j, w(i)>w(j)\}|$

definitions.statement:
For $w \in S_n$, the **descent set** is $\text{Des}(w) = \{i \in [n-1] : w(i) > w(i+1)\}$.

For $S = \{s_1 < s_2 < \cdots < s_k\} \subseteq [n-1]$, set $s_0 = 0$ and $s_{k+1} = n$. Define:
- $\alpha_n(S) = |\{w \in S_n : \text{Des}(w) \subseteq S\}|$ (at least $S$ means no descents outside $S$)
- $\beta_n(S) = |\{w \in S_n : \text{Des}(w) = S\}|$ (exactly $S$)
definitions.notes: Note the naming: $\alpha$ = 'at least' (descent set **contained in** $S$, so there are at most the descents of $S$), while $\beta$ = 'exactly $S$.' This seems reversed from the $f_{\geq}$//$f_{=}$ notation: that's because $\alpha_n(S) = f_{\leq}(S)$ (descent set **subset** of $S$) rather than $f_{\geq}$. The I-E formula still applies with the same alternating sign.

propositions.title: Derangement recurrence
propositions.proof_sketch: Consider derangements $w$ of $[n]$. Choose $w(n) = k$ for some $k \in [n-1]$ (so $w(n) \neq n$). Case 1: $w(k) = n$. Then the remaining $n-2$ values form a derangement of $[n] \setminus \{k,n\}$, giving $(n-1) D(n-2)$ such $w$. Case 2: $w(k) \neq n$. Replace $n$ by $k$ in the constraint: now positions $1,\ldots,n-1$ form a derangement of $[n-1]$ (with $k$ playing the role of $n$), giving $(n-1) D(n-1)$ such $w$.

propositions.title: Determinantal formula for $f_{=}$
propositions.statement:
Let $0 = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_k < s_{k+1} = n$ and let $g: \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \to R$ be any function into a commutative ring $R$. Suppose $f_{\leq}(S)$ (the I-E 'at-least' function) has the product form $f_{\leq}(S) = \prod_{i=0}^{k} g(s_{i+1} - s_i)$ for every $S = \{s_1,\ldots,s_k\} \subseteq [n-1]$. Then:
$$f_{=}(S) = \det\bigl[g(s_{j+1} - s_i + j - i - 1)\bigr]_{i,j=1}^{k+1}$$
(indices adjusted so the matrix is $(k+1) \times (k+1)$ with entries depending on $s_i, s_j$).

More explicitly with $s_0 = 0$, $s_{k+1} = n$: the matrix entry in row $i$, column $j$ is $g(s_{j+1} - s_i)$, where rows/columns are indexed $0, \ldots, k$.
propositions.proof_sketch: The I-E formula is $f_{=}(S) = \sum_{T \supseteq S} (-1)^{|T|-|S|} f_{\leq}(T)$. With the product structure, summing over supersets $T$ of $S$ is equivalent to, for each 'gap' $(s_i, s_{i+1})$ in $S$, independently choosing whether to refine it by inserting more points. The Leibniz expansion of the determinant exactly encodes this alternating sum over permutations (refinements).

theorems.title: Derangement formula
theorems.statement:
$$D(n) = n! \sum_{j=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^j}{j!} \approx \frac{n!}{e} \tag{2.11--2.14}$$
Also: $D(n) = (n-1)(D(n-1) + D(n-2))$ and the EGF is $\hat{D}(x) = \sum_{n \geq 0} D(n) x^n/n! = e^{-x}/(1-x)$.
theorems.proof_sketch: Apply the symmetric I-E with properties $p_i$: 'position $i$ is a fixed point.' Then $b(k) = (n-k)!$ and $D(n) = a(0) = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \binom{n}{k}(n-k)! = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k n!/k!$.

theorems.title: At-least descent count is a multinomial
theorems.statement:
For $S = \{s_1 < \cdots < s_k\} \subseteq [n-1]$ with $s_0=0$, $s_{k+1}=n$, let $c_i = s_i - s_{i-1}$ for $i=1,\ldots,k+1$. Then:
$$\alpha_n(S) = \binom{n}{c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_{k+1}} = \frac{n!}{c_1!\, c_2!\, \cdots\, c_{k+1}!} \tag{2.15}$$
theorems.proof_sketch: A permutation $w \in S_n$ has $\text{Des}(w) \subseteq S$ iff in each block $(s_{i-1}, s_i]$ of positions, $w$ is **weakly increasing**. Equivalently, $w$ is a shuffle of $k+1$ increasing runs of lengths $c_1, \ldots, c_{k+1}$. The number of such shuffles is $n! / (c_1! \cdots c_{k+1}!)$.

theorems.title: Descent-set count as a determinant
theorems.statement:
With $S = \{s_1 < \cdots < s_k\}$, $s_0 = 0$, $s_{k+1} = n$:
$$\beta_n(S) = \sum_{T \supseteq S} (-1)^{|T|-|S|} \alpha_n(T) \tag{2.15, via I-E}$$
This equals the determinant (Eq. 2.16):
$$\beta_n(S) = \det\!\left[\frac{1}{(s_{j+1} - s_i)!}\right]_{0 \leq i,j \leq k} \cdot \prod_{i=0}^{k} (s_{i+1} - s_i)! \cdot n!$$
More cleanly, factoring out row and column constants (Eq. 2.17):
$$\beta_n(S) = n! \cdot \det\!\left[\binom{n - s_i}{s_{j+1} - s_i}\right]_{0 \leq i,j \leq k}$$
theorems.proof_sketch:
Step 1: $\alpha_n(T)$ depends only on the gap lengths $t_{j+1} - t_j$. Factor it: $\alpha_n(T) = n! / \prod_j (t_{j+1}-t_j)!$. This is a product over the gaps of $T$, matching the hypothesis of Prop. 2.2.6 with $g(m) = 1/m!$.

Step 2: Apply I-E over supersets $T \supseteq S$. Each such $T$ is obtained by inserting extra breakpoints into the gaps of $S$. For each gap $(s_i, s_{i+1})$ of $S$, the contribution of inserting extra breakpoints in that gap is independent of other gaps. This independence is what gives the Leibniz (determinant) structure.

Step 3 (Eq. 2.16 → 2.17): Factor $1/\prod_i s_i!$ from row $i$ and $s_{j+1}!$ from column $j$. These telescope to absorb $n!$ and transform $1/(s_{j+1}-s_i)!$ into the binomial $\binom{n-s_i}{s_{j+1}-s_i}$ after rescaling.

theorems.title: $q$-analogue: descent set weighted by inversions
theorems.statement:
Define $\alpha_n^q(S) = \sum_{\text{Des}(w) \subseteq S} q^{\text{inv}(w)}$ (weight by inversions). Then:
$$\alpha_n^q(S) = \binom{n}{c_1, \ldots, c_{k+1}}_q \cdot \prod_i [c_i]_q! \quad\text{where } [n]_q! \cdot \binom{n}{k}_q = [n]_q! \tag{2.18--2.20}$$
More precisely, $\alpha_n^q(S) = [n]_q! / \prod_{i=1}^{k+1} [c_i]_q!$ where $c_i = s_i - s_{i-1}$.

The $q$-analogue of $\beta_n(S)$ is:
$$\beta_n^q(S) = \sum_{\text{Des}(w) = S} q^{\text{inv}(w)} = [n]_q! \cdot \det\!\left[\binom{n-s_i}{s_{j+1}-s_i}_q\right]_{0 \leq i,j \leq k} \tag{2.21}$$
theorems.proof_sketch: The inversion count for $w$ with $\text{Des}(w) \subseteq S$ decomposes: inversions come only from comparing values in different blocks. The $q$-multinomial counts such shuffles weighted by $q^{\text{inv}}$, generalizing the ordinary multinomial. Then the $q$-determinant follows from the same Leibniz-sum argument, with $g(m) = 1/[m]_q!$.

examples.title: Example 2.2.1 — Derangements via EGF
examples.content:
The EGF for derangements is $\sum_{n \geq 0} D(n) x^n / n! = e^{-x}/(1-x)$.

Since $1/(1-x) = \sum_n n! \cdot x^n/n!$ is the EGF for factorials, and $e^{-x} = \sum_k (-1)^k x^k/k!$, their product gives $D(n) = \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k n!/k!$ by the EGF convolution. Setting $y = -x$: $D(n)/n! \to 1/e$ as $n \to \infty$.

examples.title: Example 2.2.3 — Multiset permutations
examples.content:
Let $M$ be a multiset with $a_i$ copies of letter $i$, $|M| = n$. A **multiset permutation** is any arrangement of $M$. Define property $p_{ij}$: 'the $j$-th copy of letter $i$ appears in the wrong order relative to other copies of $i$' (i.e., the relative order of the $a_i$ copies of $i$ is not the natural order $1,2,\ldots,a_i$).

In the I-E setup: $b(k) = $ number of arrangements of $M$ with the relative order of at least $k$ specified letters fixed. This is $n! / \prod_i a_i!$ times a correction for the fixed constraints.

The symmetric I-E gives $a(0) = n! / \prod_i a_i!$ (the multinomial coefficient), and $b(k) = $ number of arrangements where at least $k$ 'repeats' occur.
examples.solution: The key point: $b(k)$ as defined in the text counts arrangements where at least $k$ of the ordered copies are in the 'natural' (non-repeating) order. When ALL copies of every letter are in natural order, we get the multinomial $n!/\prod a_i!$. The I-E then recovers this as the 'zero repeats' count.

examples.title: Example 2.2.4 — $\beta_8(\{1,5\})$ via determinant (Eq. 2.17)
examples.content:
Count permutations $w \in S_8$ with descent set exactly $\{1,5\}$, i.e., $w(1) > w(2) < w(3) < w(4) < w(5) > w(6) < w(7) < w(8)$.

Here $S = \{s_1, s_2\} = \{1,5\}$, so $k=2$, $s_0=0, s_1=1, s_2=5, s_3=8$. The formula gives a $3 \times 3$ determinant with entry $(i,j)$ equal to $\binom{8-s_i}{s_{j+1}-s_i}$:

$$\begin{pmatrix} \binom{8}{1} & \binom{8}{5} & \binom{8}{8} \\ \binom{7}{0} & \binom{7}{4} & \binom{7}{7} \\ 0 & \binom{3}{0} & \binom{3}{3} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 56 & 1 \\ 1 & 35 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

**Why lower-triangular entries are 0**: $\binom{n-s_i}{s_{j+1}-s_i} = 0$ whenever $s_{j+1} < s_i$ (negative top, since $n - s_i < n - s_j$, but actually the key is $s_{j+1} - s_i < 0$). This forces the matrix to be **upper Hessenberg**, making the determinant easy to compute along the bottom row.
examples.solution:
$$\det = 8(35 - 1) - 56(1 - 0) + 1(1 - 0) = 272 - 56 + 1 = \boxed{217}.$$

Verify: $\alpha_8(\{1,5\}) = \binom{8}{1,4,3} = 280$. The overcounting is from permutations with descent sets $\{1,5,j\}$ for $j \in \{2,3,4,6,7\}$ and $\{1,5,j,k\}$, etc. I-E via the determinant automatically handles all these corrections.

examples.title: Example 2.2.5 — The $q$-multinomial and why $\text{inv}(w)$ works
examples.content:
For $n=3$, $S = \{1\}$ (so $k=1$, $c_1=1$, $c_2=2$):
$$\alpha_3^q(\{1\}) = \sum_{\text{Des}(w) \subseteq \{1\}} q^{\text{inv}(w)} = [3]_q! / ([1]_q! [2]_q!) = \binom{3}{1}_q$$

The permutations with $\text{Des}(w) \subseteq \{1\}$ (i.e., $w(1) > w(2) < w(3)$ is not required; we just need no descents outside position 1, so $w$ is **increasing from position 2 onward**, meaning $w(2) < w(3)$). These are: $132\ (\text{inv}=1)$, $213\ (\text{inv}=1)$, $231\ (\text{inv}=2)$, $312\ (\text{inv}=2)$... Wait: $\{w : \text{Des}(w) \subseteq \{1\}\}$ means the only possible descent is at position 1. So $w(2) < w(3)$ is required. The 4 such permutations are: $123\ (0),\ 132\ (1),\ 213\ (1),\ 312\ (2)$. Sum: $1 + q + q + q^2 = (1+q)(1) \cdot (1+q+q^2)/(1) = [3]_q!/([1]_q![2]_q!) = \binom{3}{1}_q$. ✓

**Why $\text{inv}$ works**: inversions between positions in different blocks of $S$ account for all $q$-factors. Inversions within a single increasing block are 0. The $q$-multinomial exactly counts the inversions contributed by choosing which elements go in which block.

exercises.statement: Prove that $D(n) = n D(n-1) + (-1)^n$ for $n \geq 1$. (Use the formula $D(n) = n!\sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k/k!$ directly.)
hints: Compute $D(n) - n D(n-1)$ using the sum formula. Most terms cancel telescopically.

exercises.statement: Give a bijective proof of the recurrence $D(n) = (n-1)(D(n-1)+D(n-2))$. (Stanley hints at an explicit construction.)
hints: For a derangement $w$ of $[n]$, consider where $n$ goes. If $w(n) = k$, then either $w(k) = n$ (a transposition, leaving a derangement of $[n-2]$) or $w(k) \neq n$ (gives a derangement of $[n-1]$ by remapping $k \mapsto n$).
The bijection for case 2: given $w$ with $w(n)=k$, $w(k) \neq n$, define $w'$ on $[n-1]$ by $w'(i) = w(i)$ for $i \neq n$, $w'(k) = w(k)$ (where $k$ now represents $n$). Check $w'$ is a derangement.

exercises.statement: Verify that $\beta_6(\{2,4\}) = 6! \cdot \det \binom{6-s_i}{s_{j+1}-s_i}$ for appropriate $s_i$. Compute the $3 \times 3$ matrix explicitly and evaluate the determinant. Cross-check by computing $\alpha_6(\{2,4\})$ and subtracting the overcounts.
hints: $S = \{2,4\} \subseteq [5]$, so $s_0=0, s_1=2, s_2=4, s_3=6$. The matrix entries are $\binom{6-s_i}{s_{j+1}-s_i}$.
